content.intro: This lesson focuses on json versus yaml and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: JSON Versus YAML matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: JSON and YAML can often represent equivalent mappings, sequences, and scalar values, but conversion can change types, omit comments, expose duplicate keys, or alter formatting. Compare parsed values and document what the target tools preserve.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: Syntax differences. Whitespace and indentation. Data model differences. Strings and numeric values. Comments.; Readability. Parsing complexity. Use-case suitability.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: JSON Versus YAML
content_blocks.expected_output: This JSON value can be represented with a corresponding YAML mapping and sequence, though comments and presentation details are not part of the JSON model.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as example.json and run `python -m json.tool example.json`. This validates JSON syntax and formats the file; it does not validate a JSON Schema or application business rules.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting fixture before each test. Change one field, indentation level, parser option, or schema constraint at a time, then compare the result with the prediction.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is a reference/example, not evidence that the CodeLeaf browser executes JSON/YAML parsing, shell commands, or Python. Validate locally with a named parser or tool before relying on it.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Do not judge a conversion only by how the text looks. Parse both documents, compare values and types, and record features that cannot be represented on both sides. Confirm implementation-specific behavior against the target parser, tool version, and standards documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second synthetic fixture for “Syntax differences. Whitespace and indentation. Data model differences. Strings and numeric values. Comments.”. Predict the parsed types/result, change one relevant detail, and record whether the target tool behaved as expected. Include one invalid or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
